title: Question 3: State Primary Elections

context.text: Placed on the ballot by initiative petition: the Information for Voters labels it a law proposed by initiative petition on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026. The Legislature's Special Joint Committee on Initiative Petitions issued the legislative reports reproduced in the same booklet.

question.text: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? State Primary Elections: This proposed law would eliminate political party primaries for state elections and instead establish a system where there would be a single, all-party primary in which all candidates, regardless of their party affiliation, would be listed on one ballot, and voters could vote for any candidate on the ballot. The two candidates receiving the most votes in the primary would advance to the general election ballot. This proposed law would require candidates for governor and lieutenant governor to run and be listed jointly on the ballot in the primary. This proposed law would provide political party status to any group whose candidates for any statewide office received at least 3% of the ballots cast in the state primary.

summary.text: The measure would eliminate party primaries for state elections and replace them with a single all-party primary in which all candidates appear on one ballot and the top two vote-getters advance to the general election. Candidates for governor and lieutenant governor would run jointly, and any group whose candidates for statewide office won at least 3% of ballots cast in the state primary would receive political party status. Statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office for Administration and Finance): The proposed law has no discernible material fiscal consequences for state and municipal government finances

measure.yesMeans: A YES VOTE would eliminate separate party primaries for state elections and require a single primary in which all candidates appear on one ballot, voters could vote for any candidate, and the top two candidates would advance to the general election.
measure.noMeans: A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing primary elections.

argumentsFor.text: In the 150-word argument in favor signed by Danielle Allen of the Coalition for Healthy Democracy, as printed in the Information for Voters: "All-Party Primaries will bring accountability and transparency to Massachusetts politics by making elections more competitive, forcing politicians to listen."

argumentsAgainst.text: In the 150-word argument against signed by Vanessa A. Snow of Voter Rights MA, as printed in the Information for Voters: "This proposal would limit voter choice by allowing only two candidates to advance to November — even if they belong to the same party — reducing competition, lowering voter participation, worsening inequities, and narrowing debate."

researchNotes: Ballot text, official yes/no statements and fiscal statements are taken from the Secretary of the Commonwealth's 2026 Information for Voters booklet (PDF text extracted and checked by script). Arguments are quoted from the signed 150-word pro/con statements, which the Commonwealth states reflect the authors' opinions and are not certified as accurate. Both a signed pro and a signed con argument are printed. The booklet's own summary is the Attorney General's; the Secretary's page and Ballotpedia could not be fetched (bot protection), so the ballot list was confirmed from the booklet itself, which covers nine questions.
